To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

greta and azarcon, two lead-containing folk remedies used in Mexican-American communities, have produced cases of lead poisoning and are currently being used by a substantial proportion of Mexican-American households in the United States and Mexico.

(1) Greta and Azarcons are used in Mexican American households as a folk remedy for the culture bound syndrome empacho; (2) The incidence of use in our survey population was 10.5%; (3) Greta and azarcon are toxic substances and have been implicated as causes of lead poisoning; (4) Greta and azacon are used as a folk remedy by Mexican American households in the San Francisco Bay Area and other parts of the United States;
In summary, our research is concerned with

two issues: (1) the identification of potentially toxic substances in the ethnomedical system of the Mexican-American population, and (2) an analysis of the cultural factors which may contribute to the use of these substances.
the identification of a potential health hazard in Mexican-American communities, a hazard which has been largely overlooked by the medical community.
the identification of a toxic substance in an ethnomedical system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence to indicate that the use of greta and azarcon has declined.
the use of greta and azarcon is a major health problem for the Mexican-American community and that the use of these compounds is not a cultural practice but rather the use of a folk remedy.
the use of these substances is a significant health hazard to the community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Mexican-American folk remedies greta and azarcon are used by Mexican-Americans to treat empacho and that they are toxic to children.

we found a high incidence of use of these two toxic substances, greta and azarcon, in the Mexican-American community, and that these substances have been associated with cases of acute lead intoxication.
there is an urgent need for a more comprehensive and integrated study of the relationship between ethnomedicine and the practice of medicine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we must not only understand the cultural context in which people live and practice medicine, but also the toxicological properties of the remedies used in these practices.
we need to do more to understand the role of culture in the health of our patients.
